title: What Banks Really Look For in a Loan
summary: Lenders weigh three questions for every loan: can you repay it, will you repay it, and what happens if you don't. Here is how each one is assessed.
seoTitle: What Banks Really Look For in a Loan | Clarity
metaDescription: Lenders weigh three questions for every loan: can you repay it, will you repay it, and what happens if you don't. Here is how each one is assessed.
content:
Whether it's a residential mortgage or a commercial loan, lenders are ultimately assessing the same three questions for every applicant: can this borrower repay the loan, will they repay it, and what happens if they don't.

Can you repay it? Income and debt levels

This is where income documentation and debt-to-income ratio come in. A lender compares monthly income against existing and proposed debt payments to gauge whether the numbers leave enough room to comfortably support a new loan. See how DTI is calculated for the exact formula.

Will you repay it? Credit history

Credit history is a track record. On-time payments, how much available credit is being used, and the length and depth of credit history all factor into how a lender predicts future repayment behavior.

What if you don't? Collateral

Collateral is the lender's fallback if a loan isn't repaid — a home for a mortgage, equipment or receivables for a commercial loan. The stronger and more liquid the collateral, the more flexibility a lender may have on other terms.

Why rates differ so much between loans

The higher the perceived risk across those three questions, the higher the rate a lender is likely to charge. That's part of why a long-term, well-collateralized mortgage often carries a materially lower rate than a shorter-term, less-collateralized business loan.

Example

A 30-year mortgage backed by a home and a strong credit history might price meaningfully lower than a short-term business loan with thinner collateral and a shorter track record — the gap reflects risk, not favoritism.

Where deposits fit in

Existing account relationships, particularly deposit balances, can also influence a lender's assessment and pricing. See how deposits affect loan pricing for more on why lenders often ask borrowers to move accounts over.

The takeaway

Understanding what's actually being evaluated — repayment capacity, repayment likelihood, and downside protection — makes it easier to prepare a stronger loan application before applying. See what lenders typically review for a fuller checklist.

title: The Fed, Rate Cuts, and What Actually Changes for You
summary: Federal Reserve rate decisions get a lot of attention, but they don't affect every kind of borrowing the same way. Here is what typically moves and what doesn't.
seoTitle: The Fed, Rate Cuts, and What Actually Changes for You | Clarity
metaDescription: Federal Reserve rate decisions get a lot of attention, but they don't affect every kind of borrowing the same way. Here is what typically moves and what doesn't.
content:
Figures in this article reflect economic conditions as of August 2025 and are provided for illustration only — they are not updated in real time and should not be relied on as current data.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) typically meets eight times a year to review inflation, unemployment, GDP, and broader financial conditions, and to set the federal funds rate — the rate banks charge each other for overnight lending.

What a rate cut actually does

When the Fed lowers the federal funds rate, banks can generally borrow at a lower cost, which can translate into lower rates on certain lending products. But the effect isn't uniform across every type of borrowing.

What moves and what doesn't

  • Mortgages — priced primarily off long-term treasury yields, so they are not directly or immediately affected by a Fed rate move.
  • Lines of credit — often priced off the Prime Rate, which typically moves in step with Fed decisions.
  • Variable-rate commercial loans — also frequently tied to Prime, so these can see a more direct impact.

In other words, a Fed rate cut doesn't automatically lower an existing fixed-rate mortgage, but it can meaningfully affect variable-rate credit products.

Why the Fed sometimes holds instead of cutting

As of August 2025, several factors were commonly cited for a cautious, data-dependent approach rather than an immediate rate cut: the risk that tariffs could push inflation higher, GDP growth running below its long-run historical average, unemployment still low relative to its long-run average, and inflation trending only slightly above the Fed's 2% target. None of these factors point in a single obvious direction, which is part of why rate decisions can be hard to predict.

The takeaway

Rate decisions are driven by a mix of economic data, not by a single indicator or a fixed schedule — and their effect depends heavily on what type of loan or credit product is involved. Understanding which of your own balances are rate-sensitive is more useful than trying to predict the Fed's next move.

title: How Deposits Affect Your Loan Pricing
summary: Banks don't just take deposits and make loans separately — deposits directly lower a bank's cost of funds, which can translate into better loan pricing for borrowers who keep accounts there.
seoTitle: How Deposits Affect Your Loan Pricing | Clarity
metaDescription: Deposits lower a bank's cost of funds, which can translate into better loan pricing. Here is how the relationship between deposits and lending works.
content:
It's a common question when taking out a loan: why does a lender ask a borrower to also move their deposit accounts over? The answer comes down to how banks fund the loans they make.

Deposits are a bank's funding source

Most checking accounts pay little or no interest, which effectively gives a bank low-cost funds to lend out. A savings account paying a higher rate costs the bank more, narrowing its margin on that portion of deposits. Either way, deposits are the raw material banks use to make loans — the more deposits a bank holds, the more it generally has available to lend, and often at a lower blended cost.

Cost of funds and loan pricing

Banks typically price loans by adding a spread on top of their cost of funds. If a borrower keeps meaningful deposit balances at the same bank, that can lower the bank's overall cost of funds and give it more room to offer a sharper rate or reduced fees on that borrower's loan.

Example

If a bank's baseline cost of funds plus target spread would price a loan around 7.3%, a borrower who keeps significant checking and savings balances at that bank may see the bank price the loan more competitively, since those deposits help offset the bank's funding cost.

How banks actually make money

The core of bank profitability is the spread between what's earned on loans and what's paid out on deposits — plus non-interest income from things like wire fees, card interchange, and other services. A "free" checking account isn't really free; it's funded by what the bank earns lending out that account's balance.

Why this matters for borrowers

Keeping deposits at the bank being asked to extend a loan can genuinely improve outcomes in three ways: stronger approval odds, since the relationship gives the bank more visibility and lower risk; better pricing, since deposits lower funding costs; and potentially better rates on the deposit side too, as the relationship strengthens. Community banks in particular tend to recycle local deposits directly back into loans for local businesses and projects, so keeping deposits local can have a knock-on community effect as well.

The takeaway

Deposits and loans are not two separate products — they're connected. Consolidating accounts with a single relationship bank is one of the more overlooked ways to influence loan approval odds and pricing.

title: 5 Money Lessons Everyone Should've Learned in School
summary: Checking accounts, high-yield savings, budgeting, retirement accounts, and brokerage investing — five fundamentals that rarely get taught in a classroom.
seoTitle: 5 Money Lessons Everyone Should've Learned in School | Clarity
metaDescription: Checking accounts, high-yield savings, budgeting, retirement accounts, and brokerage investing — five fundamentals that rarely get taught in a classroom.
content:
Personal finance is rarely taught as its own subject in school, even though nearly everyone will open a checking account, build a budget, and eventually think about retirement. Financial-literacy programs that work with young adults often start with the same five fundamentals.

1. Checking accounts: where your money lives

Not all checking accounts are equal. Before setting up direct deposit, it's worth checking for monthly fees, minimum balance requirements, and whether the account offers interest or early access to a paycheck. A fee-free account with useful perks is often available even when a default account isn't offering one.

2. Savings accounts: making your money work harder

Many default savings accounts pay well under 1% APY, while high-yield savings accounts — widely available and federally insured in the same way as a standard savings account — can pay several times more.

Example

$10,000 at 0.25% APY earns about $25 a year. The same $10,000 at 3.75% APY earns about $375 a year — a meaningful difference for simply choosing a better account.

3. Budgeting: a financial GPS

Without a budget, it's hard to know monthly income, spending, or debt-to-income ratio with any accuracy. A simple spreadsheet or budgeting app is often enough to start turning vague financial anxiety into a clear, trackable picture.

4. Retirement accounts: playing the long game

A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement account that often includes a matching contribution — if an employer matches 3% and an employee contributes 3%, that match is effectively an immediate 100% return before any investment gains. An IRA offers more flexibility over what to invest in, with a choice between Roth (taxed now, grows tax-free) and Traditional (taxed later) versions; as a general rule of thumb, a Roth tends to make more sense for someone who expects their income to rise over time.

5. Brokerage accounts: building beyond retirement

Once high-interest debt is under control and retirement contributions are underway, a brokerage account allows for investing beyond retirement accounts, without contribution limits or early-withdrawal penalties. Profits are taxable and markets fluctuate, so this generally comes after an emergency fund and high-interest debt are addressed, not before.

The takeaway

None of these five steps require getting rich quickly. A well-chosen checking account, a high-yield savings account, a working budget, consistent retirement contributions, and eventually a brokerage account are the fundamentals that compound into long-term financial stability.

title: Why Your Banking Relationship Matters
summary: Apps and rate sheets aside, banking still comes down to who picks up the phone when something comes up. Here is why the relationship behind the account matters.
seoTitle: Why Your Banking Relationship Matters | Clarity
metaDescription: Apps and rate sheets aside, banking still comes down to who picks up the phone when something comes up. Here is why the relationship behind the account matters.
content:
Behind every app, portal, and rate sheet, banking still comes down to one thing: relationships. For a business owner or a household managing a major financial decision, the real test of a banking relationship is simple — when something comes up, is there someone specific to call?

Why access and trust matter

Strong banking relationships tend to share a few traits:

  • Proactive conversations before a problem becomes urgent
  • Honest feedback, even when it isn't the answer someone wants to hear
  • Terms and structure tailored to a specific situation rather than a one-size-fits-all template
  • Faster resolution, because there's already context on the relationship
  • Clear accountability, because a specific person is attached to the work

Trust compounds over time

The more a bank understands a borrower's situation — their cash flow cycle, their goals, their history — the better the guidance and the terms tend to become. That applies just as much to a growing small business as it does to a family navigating a major financial decision like a home purchase.

Why local relationships can matter more

Community banks in particular tend to lend directly back into the markets they serve. Understanding local conditions and knowing the people behind the numbers can translate into decisions that a purely transactional, call-center relationship often can't replicate.

The takeaway

Digital tools, faster payments, and automation will keep improving the banking experience, but none of it replaces a direct, trusted relationship. The strongest banking relationships remain simple: reach out, and it gets handled.
